item.content:encoded:
Well, as far as laboriousness goes, Guts itself is overlong. Among other things.

(But I didn't find it particularly nauseating? Maybe familiarity with the instances of that particular injury makes a difference. "Body horror" probably just engages my curiosity and/or empathy more than it turns my stomach.)

It's worth pointing out that I find your concept more interesting than Palahniuk's. It could hit more emotions than just "ew gross" or "woe is me I died while [EXPUNGED]", and the way you play with guilt, especially in the last lines, is a great example of that. The idea of breaking biologically-ingrained taboos…

I guess my point is: you could leave this as an (apparently effective) bit of creepypasta, or you could keep wrestling with it, and maybe get a neat little horror short story.

item.content:encoded:
Of course it doesn't, what I was saying was that I merely was trying out a different style of writing. And the laboriousness of Guts is well… I'd say that's a very subjective thing. On one hand, you're right, he does use shorter sentences, on the other hand, I find that his description is filled with adjectives. Anyway, the point is that what I was trying to do was to assault readers with this description, the number of modifiers was meant to disturb and put readers off-guard, cause them unease. Maybe I over-did it, but in the context of this story, I don't think that was a mistake per se, at most, not as well done as I had hoped it would be.

I do understand what you're saying though, I used to suffer from written diarrhea, quite badly. This story though, was more a controlled stream (eugh, pardon the image) rather than me just plonking all the adjectives I knew into the line.

item.title: (no title)
item.content:encoded:
Well, as Palahniuk said, himself, "Until you can create something that captivates people, I'd invite you to just shut up." So who am I to judge? ;) You've certainly hit the right buttons, for some readers, which is a sign that you are doing something very right.

But I still think criticism has some value, as subjective as mine is, so I'm gonna reply….

Pardon my blunt, but Guts doesn't quite work as a stylistic comparison, body horror aside. It's a hell of a lot better written, for one. The author's prose isn't laborious or sopping with adjectives; the sentences are almost staccato.

The criticism I was making is that you have too many damn modifiers. Everywhere. Convoluted can be effective; excess isn't the same thing. Let me try to illustrate by example: (examples now behind a cut because yikes wall of text)

+ show block
– hide block

"Her other hand shook as it edged towards the battered metal plate, slipped slightly in the pooling blood, and finally managed to clasp around the oozing organ, picking it up. It squelched in her grasp. Small showers of blood dripped from it, slipping from the cracks between her fingers and back into the plate, merging with the symphony of expectant silence in the operating room."

VS: "Her hand shook as it hesitated over the plate. The blood was slippery. She couldn't keep hold of the oozing thing without digging her fingers into it. It made a squelching sound, sickening loud in the silent room. She picked it up. Blood trickled down her wrist."

"the madness and darkness evaporated beneath the soothing touch of humanity, suffocated by the constricting knots of the straitjacket"

VS: "the darkness would evaporate beneath the touch of humanity, the madness choked in the knots of a straitjacket"

"And here she was, holding a pillow above the face of some woman she didn’t know, pressing it down as hands clawed at her. The woman’s body, young and lithe except for the distended belly possessing her spawn, struggled and bucked under her grip, but she held on, a strength that could come only from insane hunger pressing down her arms. The monitor rattled on the table, unplugged cord scattering about the floor, the bed shivered with the dying woman’s convulsions. Her grip upon the pillow softened as the woman struggled less and less, until finally, the flailing hands fell limply against the sides of the bed."

edit: now with more unsettling Biblical metaphor!
VS: "Here she was, pressing the pillow down as hands clawed at her. The stranger was young, her belly swollen like ripe fruit. The stranger's struggle was fierce, but hunger gave her inhuman strength. Hunger locked her arms and fingers until the knuckles whitened, even as the bed shuddered with convulsions. The distended belly quivered.

Then all was still."

….. Does using fewer words really take away from the mood or meaning of those passages?

item.content:encoded:
Mm I understand where you're coming from, I can see the convoluted descriptions being a detriment rather than a good thing. Still, I do wish to argue my stand:

The way I see it, the most important facet about this story I have written is the atmosphere of unease that I (hope) I managed to create, the sense to the reader that all is unwell. In part then, this is achieved through the graphic and long descriptions, the labored words mixing in with the disgusting sounds and imagery. The descriptions may not be entirely accurate, for example the one you pin-pointed about the spikes, but those are the closest I can come to describe the emotion in a manner I feel befitting it. When I feel a pain in my chest, it comes in sharp bursts, feeling as if something were puncturing me from the front, and each one sends a wave of emotion mixed with physical sensation to my head - thus, I used the phrase. Granted, not everyone may catch that, it is quite the personal description, but it feels right, placing it there.

On the other hand, as much as I hate to drop author names, (reminds me of Literature Class all over again), I can see supporting examples, and contradictory examples against this style of writing. For example, Roddy Doyle, who wrote a short horror story that I read recently, managed to give me a sense of unease with minimal description, mostly working through dialogue. It was simply "He bit the head off the chicken". On the flip-side, we have Chuck Palahniuk, who writes certain stories in an intensely convoluted and graphic manner, using it to disgust and make the readers uncomfortable. I defy you to read Palahniuk's "Guts" and not feel queasy - (in fact it's famous for causing more than one person to throw up and even one to faint during a public reading).

Anyway, this style of writing is not for everyone, I understand, and well, I think I can see how my descriptions are flawed. If you read my other creepypasta story, Pitter=patter (shameless promotion of it here), you'll see a much less labored descriptive style. I just felt that in this story, in this case, this form of description helped rather than hindered the tale. Thanks for the criticism and opinions, they caused me to think for a while.

Satisfyingly creepy idea— but too purple for an upvote, as is.

I mean, "She didn’t tell any of them of the mind-blowing spikes that had lodged themselves in her chest, that sparked her fire and drove her insane." That line could be from a fanfic. Mind-blowing spikes? That blow her mind and her… chest?

Plus, the squelching and the rivulets and the spray and streams and overall bloody juiciness kept the descriptions from being as sharp (and as unsettling) as they could have been. Also "nubile" should be retired from internet use (along with "lithe", possibly), and "searched online" gives me the image of an intense Google montage and should go. There's just excess in all the wrong places.

I suggest taking a razor to it… in the strictly editorial sense.
